title: Plant cells stir themselves: tiny motors drag their contents along tracks

cover.alt: A single plant cell under the microscope, golden-brown, with fine strands of cytoplasm beaded with tiny organelles running across it.

body: In many plant cells the contents are always on the move, a flow called **cytoplasmic streaming**. Motor proteins called myosins 'walk' along filaments of actin, dragging organelles with them, and the surrounding fluid gets swept along too. Big cells need this conveyor, because diffusion on its own becomes too slow as a cell gets larger. Streaming also carries chloroplasts to where the light suits them best.

slides.alt: Time-lapse microscope footage of one plant cell: strands of cytoplasm criss-cross it, beaded with tiny organelles that shift position as they stream along.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of a hair cell from a Tradescantia stamen: strands of cytoplasm run across the cell, and the tiny organelles beaded along them keep moving.

slides.question: How fast does the cytoplasm stream in the alga Chara, the fastest known?
slides.explanation: About 100 micrometres a second, a tenth of a millimetre, in cells that can grow up to 10 cm long. Streaming generally runs at 1 to 100 µm/s.

slides.heading: Spotted in 1774
slides.text: The Italian scientist Bonaventura Corti first described streaming in 1774, in the giant cells of the algae *Nitella* and *Chara*. Exactly how the motors set a whole cell flowing is still not fully understood.

slides.question: Why do large plant cells need cytoplasmic streaming?
slides.explanation: Molecules spread by diffusion quickly across a small cell, but too slowly across a large one. Streaming carries things around instead.
